questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
The two projects are mutually exclusive, so Kestrel Leisure can accept at most one of them.

(a)

Calculate the payback period of each project, giving your answers in years to two decimal places.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the average rate of return of each project, using average annual profit as a percentage of the initial investment.

[3]

(c)

Using the discount factors provided, calculate the net present value of each project.

[4]

(d)

Recalculate the net present value of Project B to include the working capital requirement, and then recommend which project Kestrel Leisure should accept. Justify your recommendation using all of your calculations.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Project A. Cumulative cash flow: after Year 1, €120 000; after Year 2, €280 000; after Year 3, €460 000. The investment of €400 000 is recovered during Year 3, when €120 000 of the €180 000 inflow is still needed. (M1)

Payback $=2+\dfrac{120\,000}{180\,000}=2.67$ years. (A1)

Project B. Cumulative cash flow: after Year 1, €60 000; after Year 2, €160 000; after Year 3, €320 000; after Year 4, €560 000. The investment is recovered during Year 4, when €80 000 of the €240 000 inflow is still needed. (M1)

Payback $=3+\dfrac{80\,000}{240\,000}=3.33$ years. (A1)

(b) Project A: total net cash flow is $120\,000+160\,000+180\,000+80\,000=540\,000$, so total profit is $540\,000-400\,000=140\,000$ and average annual profit is $\dfrac{140\,000}{4}=35\,000$. (M1)

ARR $=\dfrac{35\,000}{400\,000}\times 100=8.75\%$. (A1)

Project B: total net cash flow is €560 000, so total profit is €160 000 and average annual profit is $\dfrac{160\,000}{4}=40\,000$. ARR $=\dfrac{40\,000}{400\,000}\times 100=10.00\%$. (A1)

(c) Project A: the present values of the inflows are $120\,000(0.909)=109\,080$; $160\,000(0.826)=132\,160$; $180\,000(0.751)=135\,180$; and $80\,000(0.683)=54\,640$. The total present value is €431 060. (M1)(A1)

NPV of A $=431\,060-400\,000=+€31\,060$. (A1)

Project B: the present values are $60\,000(0.909)=54\,540$; $100\,000(0.826)=82\,600$; $160\,000(0.751)=120\,160$; and $240\,000(0.683)=163\,920$, totalling €421 220. NPV of B $=421\,220-400\,000=+€21\,220$. (A1)

(d) Project B also requires €50 000 of working capital at the start, an immediate outflow that must be discounted at the Year 0 factor of 1.000, and it recovers €50 000 at the end of Year 4, whose present value is $50\,000(0.683)=34\,150$. (M1)

Revised NPV of B $=421\,220-400\,000-50\,000+34\,150=+€5\,370$. (A1)

Recommendation: accept Project A. (A1)

Justification: Project A is superior on two of the three methods. It pays back in 2.67 years against 3.33, which matters because the loan is being serviced at 10% and a shorter payback shortens the period during which the company carries the risk of the cash flows not materialising. Its NPV is €31 060 against €5 370 for Project B once the working capital is included, and since the money is borrowed at exactly the 10% used to discount, the NPV is the method that measures the effect on shareholder wealth directly. Project B is only superior on ARR, at 10.00% against 8.75%, and that measure is misleading here because it ignores the timing of the cash flows and, as presented, ignores the working capital entirely. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The three methods produce a genuine disagreement, and the disagreement is the question. Project A is better on payback and, once the working capital is included, overwhelmingly better on NPV; Project B is better on ARR. A student who treats the three methods as interchangeable will not be able to recommend anything, because no single method ranks the projects in isolation from the company's circumstances.

The way through is to ask what the money costs. Kestrel Leisure is borrowing at 10%, and that is exactly the rate used to discount, so the NPV is measuring the effect of the investment on the value of the company after the lender has been paid. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the loan costs; a NPV of €5 370 on a €450 000 commitment is barely positive, which means Project B is close to being value-destroying once the working capital is properly accounted for. The payback figure tells the same story from the risk side: a company with debt wants cash back quickly, and Project A returns the investment almost two-thirds of a year sooner.

ARR is the odd one out, and it is worth being able to say why. It is an accounting measure that averages the profits over the life of the project, so it treats €240 000 received in Year 4 as though it were as valuable as €240 000 received in Year 1. It also ignores the working capital unless the candidate chooses to include it, and it takes no account of the size or timing of the cash flows. Here it flatters Project B precisely because B's cash flows come late and are large, which is the opposite of what a company servicing a loan should want.

The working-capital adjustment is where the question stops being routine. Working capital is not an expense: it is cash paid out that comes back. Discounting the recovery is what makes the arithmetic honest, because €50 000 returned in four years is worth €34 150 today. Students who treat the whole €50 000 as a cost will reject Project B for the wrong reason, and students who ignore it entirely will recommend it for the wrong reason.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
Tarn Valley Preserves must commit to one site, and the choice will be difficult to reverse because the lease runs for ten years.

(a)

Calculate the total annual cost at each site if demand is 220 000 units, and state which site is cheaper.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the output at which the total annual costs of the two sites are equal.

[3]

(c)

Using the probabilities given, calculate the expected annual cost at each site and comment on what your answer means for the decision.

[4]

(d)

Recommend which site Tarn Valley Preserves should choose, justifying your answer with reference to your calculations and to two qualitative factors.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Site X: total cost $=280\,000+1.80(220\,000)=280\,000+396\,000=€676\,000$. (M1)(A1)

Site Y: total cost $=140\,000+2.60(220\,000)=140\,000+572\,000=€712\,000$. (A1)

Site X is cheaper by €36 000 per year at this level of demand. (A1)

(b) Setting the two total costs equal: $280\,000+1.80q=140\,000+2.60q$. (M1)

So $140\,000=0.80q$ and $q=175\,000$ units. (M1)(A1)

Site Y is cheaper below this output and Site X above it, because Site X trades higher fixed costs for a lower variable cost per unit.

(c) Site X: $0.6(676\,000)+0.4(496\,000)=405\,600+198\,400=€604\,000$. (M1)(A1)

Site Y: $0.6(712\,000)+0.4(452\,000)=427\,200+180\,800=€608\,000$. (A1)

The expected costs differ by only €4000 per year on a commitment of more than half a million euros per year, which is well under 1% of the total. (A1) The expected-value calculation therefore does not settle the question: whichever site is chosen, the company is making almost the same bet on cost, and the decision will be decided by which risk the management team is more willing to carry rather than by the arithmetic. It is also worth noting that the expected value conceals the shape of the risk: Site Y is cheaper in the low-demand outcome and more expensive in the high-demand outcome, so choosing Y is choosing to be relatively safe if demand disappoints, while Site X is choosing to be better off if demand materialises.

(d) Recommendation: choose Site X, the city centre. (A1)

The quantitative case is narrow but consistent: Site X is €36 000 per year cheaper at the higher demand level, it has the lower expected cost at €604 000 against €608 000, and its crossover point of 175 000 units sits well below the 220 000 units that marketing considers more likely than not. Since the lease runs for ten years and the higher-demand outcome is the one the company's growth plan depends on, the cheaper variable cost is the more valuable characteristic to lock in. (A1)

The decisive qualitative factor is space. Site X has no room to expand at any price, so if demand exceeds 220 000 units the company would have to acquire a second site and duplicate management, which would destroy most of the cost advantage it has just calculated. Site Y has a large plot available now, which gives the business the option to grow without a second location. (A1)

The counter-argument is labour. Site X has a large local pool of skilled production staff, while Site Y would require training, which adds cost and time and creates a dependency on retaining the staff it trains. A preserves manufacturer depends on consistent product quality, so the availability of experienced staff reduces operational risk. On balance the expected cost difference is too small to decide the matter, and the choice between the two risks comes down to which the company fears more: a permanent capacity ceiling on a growing product, or an operating cost it cannot control. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The crossover calculation is the centre of the question and it is easy to perform mechanically without noticing what it does. There is a level of output at which the two sites cost the same, and below it the site with the lower fixed cost wins while above it the site with the lower variable cost wins. Writing that conclusion explicitly is what turns a calculation into analysis, and it is what most candidates omit.

The more interesting feature is the expected value. It is a legitimate technique and the numbers are easy, but the answer it gives is a €4000 difference on annual costs of more than €600 000, which is less than the uncertainty in any of the underlying estimates. A number that precise, resting on probabilities that are themselves a judgement, cannot bear the weight of a ten-year decision. Recognising that a calculation can be correct and still not be decisive is the analytical step the question is testing, and it is the difference between a candidate who uses a tool and one who is used by it.

That is why the qualitative factors do the real work. The decisive one is the absence of expansion space at Site X. Ten years is a long commitment for a business whose management believes demand is more likely to rise than to fall, and a site with a hard capacity ceiling turns success into a problem. The labour factor pulls the other way and a strong answer will acknowledge it rather than ignore it. The judgement is not about which factor is objectively more important but about which risk the business is better placed to absorb: a company that is already short of space is likely to value the option to expand more than a modest reduction in the risk of training costs.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
Hartswood Garden Furniture must decide whether to invest EUR 600 000 in a flow production line for its best-selling bench.

(a)

Explain two reasons why the consultant believes flow production would be suitable for the bench, and one reason why the company's other eleven products make flow production difficult.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the mean monthly demand for the bench and the demand in a peak month. Calculate the unit cost of the bench under batch production and under flow production at an annual volume of 48 000 units, and comment on the difference.

[5]

(c)

Using descriptive statistics and a decision tree, evaluate whether Hartswood should invest in the flow production line. Justify your answer with reference to capacity, storage cost and the product range.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The consultant's case for flow production rests on volume and cost. The bench is a single, standardised product made in large numbers - 48 000 units a year - and flow production is designed for exactly this: a continuous sequence of operations with little or no changeover, which spreads a high fixed cost over a large output and gives a low variable cost. Second, demand for the bench is predictable in total, and the consultant argues that a dedicated line would remove the batch changeovers that currently interrupt production. (A1)(A1)

The eleven other products are the problem. Flow production is only economic when a line can run for long periods without being stopped and altered. Hartswood makes twelve variants in total, and a flow line for the bench cannot make tables, chairs or the other bench designs. Those products must stay on batch production, so the investment would improve the cost of one product out of twelve while leaving the rest of the factory unchanged. (A1)(A1)

(b) Mean monthly demand $= 48 000 / 12 = 4 000$ benches. (A1)

Peak demand: 80% of 48 000 $= 38 400$ benches are sold in three months, so peak monthly demand $= 38 400 / 3 = 12 800$ benches. (M1)(A1)

Unit cost at 48 000 units:

Batch: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 180 000 / 48 000 = EUR 3.75$; plus variable cost EUR 18.25, giving EUR 22.00 per bench. (M1)(A1)
Flow: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 480 000 / 48 000 = EUR 10.00$; plus variable cost EUR 10.00, giving EUR 20.00 per bench. (A1)

Comment: at 48 000 units flow production is EUR 2.00 a bench cheaper, a saving of EUR 96 000 a year, and the crossover point at which flow becomes cheaper is $(EUR 480 000 - EUR 180 000) / (EUR 18.25 - EUR 10.00) = 36 364$ benches. Since annual demand is 48 000, the arithmetic appears to favour flow - but this comparison ignores the constraint that the flow line's capacity of 8 000 benches a month imposes on a seasonal product.

(c) Indicative evaluation, using descriptive statistics and a decision tree.

The descriptive statistics show why the annual average is the wrong basis for the decision. Mean monthly demand is 4 000 benches, but peak monthly demand is 12 800 and off-season demand is about 1 067. The range is therefore about 11 733 benches a month. The flow line can make only 8 000 a month, so in each of the three peak months it is short by $12 800 - 8 000 = 4 800$ benches. Over the three months the shortfall is 14 400 benches, all of which must be made in advance and stored. (M1)(A1)

Storage costs EUR 3 a bench a month, and the consultant expects an average holding period of four months: $14 400 \times EUR 3 \times 4 = EUR 172 800$ a year. The EUR 96 000 saving from flow production is therefore more than wiped out, leaving flow production EUR 76 800 a year more expensive than batch at the higher demand level. (A1)

The decision tree makes the same point under uncertainty. Marketing estimates a 0.6 probability that demand is 48 000 and a 0.4 probability that it is 30 000.

Batch production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 18.25 \times 48 000 = EUR 1 056 000$; at 30 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 547 500 = EUR 727 500$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 056 000 + 0.4 \times EUR 727 500 = EUR 924 600$. (M1)(A1)

Flow production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 10 \times 48 000 = EUR 960 000$, plus storage of EUR 172 800, giving EUR 1 132 800. At 30 000, peak monthly demand is $0.8 \times 30 000 / 3 = 8 000$, which exactly equals the line's capacity, so no storage is needed and cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 300 000 = EUR 780 000$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 132 800 + 0.4 \times EUR 780 000 = EUR 991 680$. (M1)(A1)

Batch production has the lower expected cost, by EUR 67 080, and the conclusion does not depend on the probabilities: flow is more expensive in the high-demand state and also more expensive in the low-demand state, so no plausible weighting reverses it.

The flow line would also commit EUR 600 000, would be difficult to change over, and could not make the other eleven products. Conclusion: Hartswood should not invest in the flow line. A stronger answer will note that the same analysis would justify revisiting flow production if the company could smooth demand, reduce the product range, or add a second line to raise peak capacity.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the obvious quantitative answer is the wrong one. At 48 000 units a year the flow line costs EUR 20 a bench against EUR 22 for batch, a saving of EUR 96 000, and the crossover point of 36 364 benches is comfortably below the annual volume. On that arithmetic the investment looks clearly worthwhile. The mistake is to compare costs at an annual volume when the constraint binds monthly.

The lever is that the correct operations method is determined by the volume per production run, not by the annual average. The bench sells 48 000 units a year - 4 000 a month on average - but 80% of that volume is sold in three months, so the peak month requires 12 800 benches and the flow line can make 8 000. The shortfall of 4 800 a month must be produced in advance and stored. Storage of 14 400 benches at EUR 3 a bench a month for an average of four months costs EUR 172 800, which is nearly twice the EUR 96 000 saving the flow line creates. The method that is cheapest per unit is not the method that is cheapest to run.

The decision tree reinforces the conclusion and shows that it is robust. Flow is more expensive in both demand states, so the recommendation does not depend on the 0.6 probability. That is a stronger result than a single expected-value calculation would give, and it is worth saying so.

The second constraint - the twelve product variants - is there to show that the arithmetic is not the only obstacle. Flow production is only economic when a line can run without changeover, and Hartswood's range means eleven products would remain on batch. The investment would improve the cost of one product out of twelve while adding EUR 600 000 of fixed cost.

Classic wrong turns: comparing unit costs at the annual volume and ignoring capacity; dividing annual demand by twelve and using 4 000 as the monthly requirement; computing the decision tree without the storage cost; and concluding that flow must be better because 'higher volume means lower unit cost'.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.topic: Units 3 and 5: Finance and accounts; Operations management
questions.question:
The proposed campaign would add €54 000 per year to fixed costs and is expected to change the sales mix to 60% supermarket / 40% online.

(a)

Calculate VF's weighted average contribution per unit at the current sales mix, and hence its break-even level of output.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the break-even level of output and the margin of safety at a volume of 620 000 units if the campaign achieves the expected 60 / 40 mix. Comment on why this result differs from the marketing director's claim.

[5]

(c)

Using the finance director's probabilities, calculate the expected annual profit both with and without the campaign. Evaluate, with reference to one stakeholder group and one non-financial factor, whether VF should launch the campaign.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) Contribution per unit = selling price − all variable costs.

Supermarket: $3.20-1.85-0.00=\textbf{€1.35}$ (A1)

Online: $5.00-1.85-1.10=\textbf{€2.05}$ (A1)

Weighted average contribution $=0.78(1.35)+0.22(2.05)=1.053+0.451=\textbf{€1.504 per unit}$ (M1)

$$\text{Break-even output}=\frac{\text{fixed costs}}{\text{contribution per unit}}=\frac{486\,000}{1.504}=323\,138\approx\textbf{323 000 units}$$ (A1)

(b) New weighted average contribution $=0.60(1.35)+0.40(2.05)=0.81+0.82=\textbf{€1.63 per unit}$ (M1)

New fixed costs $=486\,000+54\,000=\textbf{€540 000}$ (A1)

$$\text{New break-even output}=\frac{540\,000}{1.63}=331\,288\approx\textbf{331 000 units}$$ (A1)

$$\text{Margin of safety}=\frac{620\,000-331\,288}{620\,000}\times100=\textbf{46.6\%}$$ (A1)

The marketing director is right that contribution per unit rises, from €1.504 to €1.63. She is wrong that break-even falls: it rises, from about 323 000 to about 331 000 units, because fixed costs increase by 11.1% while weighted contribution increases by only 8.4%. The margin of safety also falls, from 47.9% to 46.6%. (A1)

(c) Profit = (volume × weighted contribution) − fixed costs.

*Without the campaign (contribution €1.504, fixed €486 000):*

  • at 620 000 units: $620\,000(1.504)-486\,000=932\,480-486\,000=\textbf{€446 480}$
  • at 480 000 units: $480\,000(1.504)-486\,000=721\,920-486\,000=\textbf{€235 920}$

$$\text{EV}=0.6(446\,480)+0.4(235\,920)=267\,888+94\,368=\textbf{€362 256}$$ (M1)(A1)

*With the campaign (contribution €1.63, fixed €540 000):*

  • at 620 000 units: $620\,000(1.63)-540\,000=1\,010\,600-540\,000=\textbf{€470 600}$
  • at 480 000 units: $480\,000(1.63)-540\,000=782\,400-540\,000=\textbf{€242 400}$

$$\text{EV}=0.6(470\,600)+0.4(242\,400)=282\,360+96\,960=\textbf{€379 320}$$ (M1)(A1)

The campaign has the higher expected profit by €17 064, about 4.7% of the expected profit without it. (A1)

*Evaluation.* On expected value the campaign is justified, and it is more robust than the margin of safety suggests: because the campaign is better in both states of the world (€470 600 > €446 480, and €242 400 > €235 920), the decision does not actually depend on which probability is correct. The break-even volume *of the change itself* is $54\,000\div(1.63-1.504)=428\,571$ units, and both volume scenarios exceed it. (A1)

However the expected-value calculation hides a step change rather than a smooth one. Supermarket buyers are the stakeholder group at risk: they supply 60% of volume even after the shift, and their reaction to a supplier promoting direct-to-consumer sales is not a 40%-chance event — it is a decision they either make or do not. If delisting removed the supermarket channel entirely, the 480 000-unit scenario would be optimistic. Set against that, a non-financial factor pulls the other way: chilled single-household delivery carries a markedly higher carbon footprint per unit than palletised supermarket distribution, which sits awkwardly with the sustainability positioning of a plant-based brand and could damage the very customers the campaign targets.

Conclusion (AO3): a supported recommendation. The expected gain of €17 064 is thin relative to a channel-specific risk that the model does not capture, so a full campaign is hard to justify on these numbers; the stronger recommendation is to test the online offer in a limited region, or to grow online volume without advertising it to supermarket customers, so that the contribution gain is captured without triggering the delisting risk. (A1)
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a trap that is invisible until the arithmetic is done. Almost every student — and, in the scenario, the marketing director — reasons that a higher contribution per unit must lower break-even. It does not, because the campaign buys that higher contribution with €54 000 of extra fixed costs, and break-even is a ratio of the two. Break-even rises and the margin of safety falls, which looks like a clear argument against the campaign.

The twist is that break-even is the wrong decision criterion here. VF sells 620 000 units against a break-even of about 330 000, so it operates far above the break-even point; in that region what matters is total contribution, not the level at which profit becomes zero. Expected profit is higher with the campaign in *both* volume states, which means the conclusion is insensitive to the probability estimates — a much stronger argument than the €17 064 figure alone suggests.

The evaluation mark separates description from judgement. Naming 'supermarket buyers' as a stakeholder earns nothing; observing that their response is a step change the probability model cannot represent does. And the sustainability point is not decoration: chilled home delivery is genuinely more carbon-intensive per unit than palletised freight, so the campaign works against the positioning of the product it is promoting.

The indifference volume makes the robustness claim exact, and it is worth stating. Because the same contribution and fixed costs apply in both volume states, the campaign's advantage does not depend on the probabilities at all: it is the better choice at any volume above the point where $1.63V - 540\,000 = 1.504V - 486\,000$, that is $V = 54\,000 / 0.126 = 428\,571$ units. Both states lie above that threshold, so the recommendation is robust - but the low state of 480 000 units sits only about 12% clear of it, which is why the answer is a qualified yes rather than a comfortable one. A candidate who reaches this point has shown that the decision turns on the volume the campaign can hold, not on the probability of the downturn.

Classic wrong turns: using €1.70 (the unweighted average of €1.35 and €2.05); treating the 22% online share as a cost rather than a mix weight; and concluding 'yes' purely from the higher expected value without acknowledging the channel risk.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 1.2 Types of business entities; 1.4 Stakeholders; 1.5 External environment
questions.question:
Marisol must decide whether to accept Dev's investment.

(a)

Explain two features of a private limited company that would help the business expand, compared with Marisol remaining a sole trader.

[4]

(b)

Using STEEPLE analysis, analyse one external factor from the case that could affect Marisol's decision.

[4]

(c)

Evaluate whether Marisol's objectives and Dev's objectives can be reconciled if she accepts the investment.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) Award two explained features:

  • Access to finance through share capital. As a private limited company the business can raise capital by issuing shares to new investors (and, unlike a sole trader, does not depend on Marisol's personal savings or retained profit). This matters because three new sites require far more than the €94 000 of annual profit Marisol currently reinvests. (A1)(A1)
  • Separate legal personality and limited liability. The company is a legal person in its own right, so it can own property, sign leases and borrow in its own name, and the shareholders' liability is limited to what they have invested. This matters because expansion into three leased sites would otherwise expose Marisol personally to unlimited liability for those commitments. (A1)(A1)
  • Also creditable: continuity of existence (the business survives changes in ownership, which matters given Dev's plan to sell), and the ability to bring in non-executive expertise through the board.

(b) Award up to four marks for one factor, analysed. For example:

  • Legal (or Economic) — the landlord's refusal to renew the lease. STEEPLE identifies the *legal* environment as an external constraint on property and tenancy. If the original site — the source of all current profit and the brand's home — must close next year, then Marisol's implicit objective of preserving the business she built is unachievable by doing nothing. This *strengthens* the case for accepting investment, because a second site would be needed simply to survive. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
  • Alternatively: Social — changing consumer demand for independent bakeries, or the expectations of her staff, who want promotion opportunities; or Economic — the cost of fit-out and the interest rate environment affecting any borrowing. Credit any factor that is genuinely external, named as a STEEPLE category, and linked to the decision.

(c) Indicative evaluation:

The conflict is real. Marisol is a sole trader for reasons that are not financial: she has repeatedly declined expansion, and her own words ("it stops being my bakery") show that control and identity are her objectives. Dev's objective is explicit — build and sell within five years. These are different definitions of success: Marisol wants to keep a business, Dev wants to exit one. (A1)(A1)

Where they overlap. Both want the business to grow and be more profitable; three more sites would give her two supervisors the promotion they want and would solve the lease problem; and Marisol's 60% holding means she is not a passive minority — she retains majority control of ordinary decisions, and as a director she would shape how expansion happens. On a narrow reading, growth and profitability are compatible with both objectives for the first few years. (A1)(A1)

Why the reconciliation is fragile. The 60/40 split protects Marisol only until Dev decides to sell: a buyer would want control, and Dev's five-year exit plan means that in five years Marisol's 60% sits inside a business someone else has chosen. Objectives also diverge on *how* to grow — Marisol avoids borrowing and grows from retained profit, while three sites in two years requires exactly the speed and risk she has spent nine years avoiding. And if the new sites fail, limited liability protects her personal assets but not the business she identifies with. (A1)

Conclusion. The objectives can be reconciled *only* if the terms change: a shareholders' agreement giving Marisol a veto over any sale of the business, or an agreed timetable that ties the exit to her own retirement. Without such protections, accepting the investment means trading an objective she actually holds (independence) for one she has never expressed (capital growth). On the evidence of the case, Marisol should either negotiate control over the exit, or decline and seek a smaller, debt-funded second site that lets her keep both the business and her independence. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Part (a) is the accessible entry point and most students handle it well. The question is designed so that (a) and (c) pull in opposite directions, and that is the whole point.

Having just explained in (a) why a private limited company is *better* for expansion, the natural answer to (c) is 'yes, they can be reconciled — convert and grow'. That answer is wrong, and not because the analysis in (a) is wrong. It is wrong because the objectives are about different things: Marisol's objective is control and identity, Dev's is a profitable exit. Converting to a company solves the finance problem; it does nothing about the fact that Dev intends to sell in five years and Marisol has spent nine years avoiding exactly that.

The detail that separates a strong answer from a competent one is the 60/40 split. Holding 60% looks like control, and for operating decisions it is. But Dev's exit plan means the *ownership* changes in five years regardless, and a buyer acquiring Dev's 40% would almost certainly demand a path to full control. A majority shareholding protects Marisol from being outvoted; it does not protect her from being out-negotiated at the point of sale.

The case also contains a fact that students routinely overlook: the landlord's decision. Without it, 'do nothing' is a viable option — Marisol keeps her profitable shop and declines. With it, the status quo is not stable, and any evaluation that assumes she can simply carry on has missed it. That is why part (b) asks for STEEPLE rather than a stakeholder map: the pressure here is external, not internal.

Classic wrong turns: describing unlimited liability as a *disadvantage* of the sole trader without linking it to the three new leases; treating Dev's investment offer as an external factor; and concluding 'she should accept because 60% means she is still in charge'.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
The founders must decide how to respond to rising staff turnover and the missed deadlines.

(a)

Describe two features of a flat organisational structure, and explain one drawback of keeping it as a business grows from 12 to 48 employees.

[4]

(b)

Using one motivation theory, explain why the 5% pay rise is unlikely to solve the turnover problem.

[5]

(c)

Evaluate whether the founders should require all staff to work from the office five days a week.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Features — award two:

  • Few or no levels of hierarchy between staff and the owners, so there is a wide span of control and a short chain of communication. (A1)
  • Decision-making is decentralised / delegated: designers choose their own projects and report directly to the founders rather than through managers. (A1)

Drawback — award one explained:

  • Role ambiguity and lack of accountability. With no manager assigning responsibility, two designers can each assume the other is leading — which is exactly what happened on the two late projects. At 12 people informal coordination works because everyone can see what everyone else is doing; at 48 it does not. (A1)(A1)
  • Also creditable: the founders' span of control has become unmanageable (48 direct reports); no appraisal system means no feedback or development; no promotion path, which is what the exit interviews identified; slower decision-making because everything escalates to two people.

(b) Using Maslow's hierarchy of needs (or Herzberg's two-factor theory):

  • Maslow arranges needs in a hierarchy: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualisation, and a need only motivates when the level below it is substantially satisfied. (A1)
  • Kestrel's designers are paid 8% above the market rate, so their lower-order needs are comfortably met. (A1)
  • The exit interviews point to a higher-order need that is unmet: recognition and the esteem that comes with a more senior role, and the self-actualisation of developing a career. Maslow's point is that a satisfied need stops motivating — so adding more of what is already satisfied (pay) will not address a deficit at a higher level. (A1)(A1)
  • Hence the 5% rise is likely to be received as fair but not motivating; the turnover is driven by the absence of a promotion path, which money does not create. (A1)

Using Herzberg instead (credit equally): pay is a hygiene factor — its absence causes dissatisfaction, but its presence does not motivate. Pay is already above market, so the hygiene factor is satisfied. The motivators are recognition, responsibility and advancement; the flat structure offers none of the last, which is why designers leave. *(Award the same marks for a correctly applied Herzberg analysis.)*

(c) Indicative evaluation:

Case for requiring five days in the office: the founders' argument is not baseless — design work benefits from spontaneous critique, and the two late projects both arose from a coordination failure that co-location would probably have surfaced earlier; new and junior staff learn faster when they can see senior designers working; and the founders, as owners, have a legitimate interest in how the studio's culture develops. (A1)(A1)

Case against: 71% of designers want three days at home, and this is the group the studio is currently losing — the three leavers cited career issues, and imposing a policy that 71% have explicitly rejected risks converting a career-structure problem into a mass resignation problem. (A1) For experienced designers whose pay is already above market, flexibility is a non-financial motivator, and removing it removes the one thing the studio currently offers that a larger agency cannot. (A1)

Conclusion: the five-day requirement addresses a real problem (coordination) with the wrong tool, and it does so at the worst possible moment. The better response is to introduce *some* structure — project leads with named responsibility, and a promotion path — while allowing hybrid work on the 71%'s preferred pattern, with a fixed day or two when the whole studio is in. That separates the two issues the founders have conflated: coordination is a management problem, and attendance is a motivation problem. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The case is built so that the obvious answer to each part is the wrong one, and in each case the evidence that shows it is wrong is sitting in the stimulus.

Part (a): flat structures are usually taught as modern and desirable, and the founders' justification ('creative people hate being managed') sounds enlightened. The two late projects are the counter-evidence, and they are there because role ambiguity is the specific failure mode of a flat structure at scale. Twelve people can coordinate by looking around the room; forty-eight cannot. Students who answer (a) by praising flat structures lose the two application marks.

Part (b) is where the theory has to do work. Both Maslow and Herzberg make the same prediction here, and both explain why a pay rise fails: once pay is above market it is a satisfied need (Maslow) or a satisfied hygiene factor (Herzberg), and neither theory says that adding more of a satisfied lower-level input produces motivation. The 8% figure is in the case precisely so that students can make this argument with evidence rather than assertion. The common weak answer is 'money isn't everything', which is a slogan, not a theory.

Part (c) is the payoff. The founders have one instrument — authority — and are applying it to a problem it cannot solve. The 71% figure is the trap: requiring five days in the office is not just ineffective, it is actively dangerous at the moment the studio is already losing people. And the deeper point, available to stronger candidates, is that the coordination failure and the attendance question are separate issues. Naming project leads fixes the late deliveries without touching working patterns at all — which means the five-day requirement is not even necessary for its own stated purpose.

Classic wrong turns: describing a tall structure instead of a flat one; using Herzberg but labelling pay as a motivator; and evaluating (c) purely on work-life balance without addressing the founders' coordination argument.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 3.5 Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis; 3.7 Cash flow
questions.question:
The finance director must decide whether the business can meet the supplier's new 14-day terms.

(a)

Calculate the gross profit margin and the net profit margin for the year ended 31 December 2026.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the current ratio and the acid test (liquid) ratio at 31 December 2026.

[4]

(c)

Using your calculations in (a) and (b) together with the cash-flow data, analyse whether Harbour Bikes Ltd can meet the supplier's new 14-day payment terms.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a)

$$\text{Gross profit margin}=\frac{\text{gross profit}}{\text{revenue}}\times100=\frac{736}{1840}\times100=40.0\%$$ (M1)(A1)

$$\text{Net profit margin}=\frac{\text{net profit}}{\text{revenue}}\times100=\frac{240}{1840}\times100=13.0\%$$ (M1)(A1)

(b)

Current assets $=210+165+48=423$ (€000); current liabilities $=132$ (€000).

$$\text{Current ratio}=\frac{423}{132}=3.20\ (\text{or }3.20:1)$$ (M1)(A1)

$$\text{Acid test ratio}=\frac{\text{current assets}-\text{inventory}}{\text{current liabilities}}=\frac{423-210}{132}=\frac{213}{132}=1.61$$ (M1)(A1)

(c) Indicative analysis:

The profitability and liquidity figures look strong. A gross margin of 40% and a net margin of 13% show a healthy business, and a current ratio of 3.20 with an acid test of 1.61 is well above the textbook benchmarks of 2:1 and 1:1. On these figures alone, the business looks able to absorb a change in payment terms. (A1)

But the ratios measure a point in time, and the trend is the problem. The cash-flow summary shows net cash from operations of €186 000 being more than consumed by investing (€140 000) and financing (€60 000) outflows, so cash *fell* by €14 000 over the year, from €62 000 to €48 000. (A1)(A1) A business whose cash balance is falling while it is profitable is growing faster than its working capital can support.

The 14-day terms are the real test. Payables of €132 000 currently represent 45 days of purchases; requiring payment in 14 days means settling the same purchases roughly 31 days earlier. The cash tied up is about

$$132\times\frac{31}{45}=\€91\ 000,$$

which must be found immediately, as a one-off, on top of ongoing trading. (A1)(A1) Against a closing cash balance of €48 000, that cannot be paid from cash. Even if the transition itself were a one-off, the change permanently raises the working capital requirement: the business would in future pay roughly 31 days earlier on every order, so the €91 000 is not recovered once the change has been absorbed. Meeting the terms therefore requires a permanent source of finance, not merely a temporary adjustment.

So where does that leave the ratios? The acid test of 1.61 looks reassuring, but €165 000 of the liquid assets are trade receivables — cash that has not yet arrived — and the inventory of €210 000 cannot be used to pay a supplier at all. The current ratio of 3.20 is flattered by that inventory. (A1)

Conclusion. The business is profitable but illiquid in the short term, and it cannot meet 14-day terms from its own resources without first slowing its investment spending, negotiating a longer period to phase in the change, accelerating receivables collection, or arranging an overdraft. The ratios in (a) and (b) describe the business it has been; the cash-flow statement describes what is happening to it now — and for this decision the cash flow is the relevant evidence.
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a genuine and very common business situation: a profitable company that runs out of cash. The trap is that every ratio the student has been taught says the business is fine.

A 40% gross margin, a 13% net margin, a current ratio of 3.2 and an acid test of 1.61 — all above benchmark. A student who stops there concludes that Harbour Bikes can easily absorb the change. The evidence that says otherwise is in the cash-flow statement, which is the one document the ratios do not summarise: operations generated €186 000, but investing and financing consumed €200 000, so cash *fell* by €14 000 over the year.

The second step is quantifying the shock. Payables of €132 000 represent 45 days; paying in 14 means finding about 31 days' worth of purchases early — roughly €91 000, as a one-off, immediately. Against €48 000 of cash, that is not feasible, and the ratios cannot help because the assets they count are not spendable: €210 000 of inventory cannot be handed to a supplier, and €165 000 of receivables is money customers have not yet paid.

The generalisable lesson — and the reason this is worth six marks — is that ratios are a snapshot and cash flow is a film. For any decision about *timing* (can we pay in 14 days rather than 45?), the snapshot is the wrong evidence, however healthy it looks. That is also why the acid test is the more informative of the two liquidity ratios here but is still not sufficient: it correctly strips out inventory, but it still treats receivables as if they were cash.

Classic wrong turns: including inventory in the acid test; concluding from the 40% gross margin that the business is 'profitable so it can pay'; and treating the €48 000 closing balance as if it were available in full when it is already committed to ongoing trading.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 4.4 Market research; 4.5 The marketing mix (price, product)
questions.question:
Vireo must choose a launch price.

(a)

(i) Calculate the weekly revenue at each of the four prices and identify the revenue-maximising price.

(ii) Calculate the weekly contribution at each price and identify the contribution-maximising price. Comment on the difference between your two answers.

[6]

(b)

Explain the difference between primary and secondary market research, and evaluate the reliability of the agency's data.

[4]

(c)

Using two elements of the marketing mix other than price, evaluate how Vireo should position the product.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) (i) Revenue $=$ price $\times$ demand:

| Price (€) | Demand | Weekly revenue (€) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.50 | 24 000 | 36 000 |
| 2.00 | 19 000 | 38 000 |
| 2.50 | 13 500 | 33 750 |
| 3.00 | 7 000 | 21 000 |

(A1) for at least three correct revenue figures, (A1) for identifying €2.00 as the revenue-maximising price.

(ii) Contribution per unit $=$ price $-\,0.85$; weekly contribution $=$ contribution per unit $\times$ demand:

| Price (€) | Contribution per unit (€) | Demand | Weekly contribution (€) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.50 | 0.65 | 24 000 | 15 600 |
| 2.00 | 1.15 | 19 000 | 21 850 |
| 2.50 | 1.65 | 13 500 | 22 275 |
| 3.00 | 2.15 | 7 000 | 15 050 |

(A1) for correct contribution per unit, (A1) for at least three correct weekly contributions, (A1) for identifying €2.50.

Comment: the two criteria disagree. Revenue is maximised at €2.00 but contribution at €2.50. (A1) Maximising revenue ignores the fact that every extra bottle sold also costs €0.85 to make: cutting the price from €2.50 to €2.00 sells 5 500 more bottles a week and raises revenue by €4 250, but it *lowers* weekly contribution by €425, from €22 275 to €21 850. A business with fixed costs to cover should choose on contribution, not revenue.

(b) Primary research is data collected first-hand for this specific purpose (surveys, focus groups, observation, test marketing). Secondary research is data that already exists and was collected for another purpose (market reports, government statistics, competitor accounts). (A1)(A1)

Evaluation of the agency's data — award up to two:

  • Sample size and location. 400 respondents is reasonable, but all four supermarkets are in the city centre, so the sample under-represents suburban and rural shoppers whose price sensitivity may differ. (A1)
  • Timing. Tuesday 09:00–11:00 captures mainly retirees, shift workers and parents with pre-school children — not the working population who buy most sparkling water. This is a systematic sampling bias, not random error, and increasing the sample would not fix it. (A1)
  • Stated preference vs actual behaviour. Asking how many bottles someone *would* buy at a price is hypothetical; people systematically overstate their willingness to pay in surveys, so the demand at €3.00 is especially likely to be optimistic. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation, using two of product, promotion, place, people, process, physical evidence:

  • Product. At €2.50 Vireo is *above* the market leader's €2.20, so the product must visibly justify a premium — distinctive packaging, a genuine fruit content claim, or a flavour range the leader does not offer. Without that, the same demand curve at a higher price is unachievable. (A1)(A1)
  • Place. A premium position requires distribution consistent with it: independent cafés, delis and higher-end supermarkets rather than deep-discount chains, where appearing alongside cheaper own-label water would undermine the price. (A1)(A1)
  • Promotion. Launch communications should explain *why* the product costs more (ingredients, provenance), since the price itself cannot; social media and in-store sampling suit a new brand with a €180 000 budget better than television. (A1)(A1)

Award up to two marks per element, for a maximum of four. The evaluation must link the mix element back to the premium price established in (a) — generic descriptions of the seven Ps earn nothing.
questions.explanation:
The arithmetic in (a) is straightforward; the insight is that the two obvious criteria disagree, and that only one of them is the right basis for a decision.

Revenue maximisation is the instinctive choice — it is what 'selling more' looks like — but it ignores the cost of making each additional bottle. At €1.50 the company sells 24 000 bottles and takes €36 000; at €2.50 it sells 13 500 and takes only €33 750, yet earns *more* (€22 275 against €15 600) because each sale contributes €1.65 rather than €0.65. The gap between €2.00 (revenue-maximising) and €2.50 (contribution-maximising) is the whole point of the part. The qualification worth noting is that contribution is the correct criterion *only because* fixed costs do not vary with the price chosen; if they did, profit rather than contribution would be the target.

Part (b) is where students who have learned 'primary is data you collect yourself' get a rude shock. The question is not what the research type is but whether the data can be trusted, and the method description is deliberately full of holes: four city-centre supermarkets excludes most of the market, and Tuesday morning excludes anyone at work. The second of these is the more important, because it is a *systematic* bias — surveying 4 000 people at 09:00 on a Tuesday would reproduce it exactly. And the hypothetical format ('how many would you buy at €X?') reliably overstates demand at high prices, which is precisely where the demand curve matters most for a premium launch.

That leaves part (c) in an interesting position: the numbers say €2.50, the data supporting them are shaky, and €2.50 is above the market leader. So the marketing mix has to carry the premium — the product must look worth more and the distribution must not contradict the price. Students who recommend a premium price and then suggest discount-channel distribution have not seen the connection.

Classic wrong turns: confusing contribution with profit; assuming the revenue-maximising price is also the profit-maximising one; and criticising the survey's *size* while missing its timing bias.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
Bramble Furniture operates a single factory and intends to increase output by 25% without changing the productivity of each employee.

(a)

Calculate the labour turnover rate and the absenteeism rate for the year.

[4]

(b)

Calculate how many production staff Bramble must recruit during the coming year to reach the planned output, and the total recruitment and training cost of doing so.

[4]

(c)

Explain, using one theory of motivation, why the 4% pay rise is unlikely to reduce labour turnover on its own.

[3]

(d)

Using your calculations, evaluate whether the 4% pay rise is a good use of the company's money.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Labour turnover $=\dfrac{\text{number of staff leaving}}{\text{average number of staff}}\times 100=\dfrac{96}{480}\times 100=20\%$. (M1)(A1)

Absenteeism $=\dfrac{\text{days lost}}{\text{total possible working days}}\times 100=\dfrac{6912}{480\times 240}\times 100=\dfrac{6912}{115\,200}\times 100=6\%$. (M1)(A1)

(b) Productivity per employee is $\dfrac{96\,000}{480}=200$ units per year. (M1)

To produce 120 000 units at the same productivity, Bramble needs $\dfrac{120\,000}{200}=600$ staff, an increase of 120. (A1)

In addition, the 96 staff who leave in a typical year must be replaced simply to stand still, so the total number of recruits is $120+96=216$. (M1)

At €3300 plus €900 per hire, the cost is $216\times 4200=€907\,200$. (A1) This figure assumes that each new employee reaches the current output of 200 units in the first year; new recruits typically take time to reach full productivity, so the true requirement may exceed 600 staff or the output fall short in the short run.

(c) Herzberg's two-factor theory distinguishes hygiene factors, which prevent dissatisfaction, from motivators, which create satisfaction. Pay is a hygiene factor: if it is too low it causes dissatisfaction, but improving it beyond a level the employees regard as acceptable does not generate motivation. (M1)

The 4% rise moves pay from below the acceptable level to about the acceptable level, or simply raises it where pay was already acceptable, so at best it removes a source of dissatisfaction rather than creating a reason to stay. If the real causes of leaving are the repetitiveness of the work, the absence of promotion opportunities, or poor supervision and working conditions, those are the motivators and they are untouched by the rise. (M1) Employees who are leaving for a better career or for more varied work will continue to do so, because the factor that would change their mind is not the one that has been altered. (A1)

(d) The 4% rise costs $480\times 28\,000\times 0.04=€537\,600$ per year, and it is a permanent addition to the pay bill. (M1)

The turnover it is intended to reduce costs about $96\times 3300=€316\,800$ per year to manage. (A1) Even if the rise eliminated turnover completely, which Herzberg's theory suggests it will not, the company would be spending €537 600 to avoid at most €316 800, so the measure cannot pay for itself on these figures. In any case the company must recruit 216 people this year because 120 of them are needed for the expansion, not because of turnover, so the pay rise would not remove that cost either. A 4% rise is also a permanent, across-the-board commitment, whereas recruitment costs are incurred only when staff actually leave; if the turnover rate were to fall for other reasons, the company would be locked into the higher pay bill with no offsetting saving. The money would be better spent on the motivators identified in part (c), or on reducing the €907 200 recruitment and training bill by improving retention through job design and progression. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question is arranged so that the arithmetic quietly condemns the decision. The pay rise looks modest as a percentage, but 4% of a payroll for 480 people is €537 600 a year and it recurs, while the turnover it is meant to cure costs about €316 800 a year. The comparison is never requested directly, which is why it separates candidates who calculate from candidates who use their calculations: the numbers are already on the page and the judgement requires putting them next to each other.

There is a second trap in part (b). The recruitment requirement has two components, and only one of them is caused by turnover. A company that is growing must hire for growth as well as for replacement, and the total — 216 people in a year for a workforce of 480 — is large enough to make the point that retention and recruitment are separate problems with separate solutions. A candidate who reports only the 120 needed for expansion has answered a smaller question than the one asked.

The motivation theory does real work here rather than being decoration. Pay is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's terms, and the theory predicts exactly the observed outcome: the pay rise removes a possible source of dissatisfaction without creating a reason to stay. That is not an argument against paying people properly; it is an argument against expecting money to solve a problem caused by the nature of the work. The same logic explains why the absenteeism figure matters too — 6% of working days lost is a symptom of something in the working environment, and no pay rise addresses it.

A strong answer will notice that the company has two problems, not one. It must grow, which requires recruitment and training at a cost of €907 200 this year, and it must retain, which a permanent pay rise will not achieve on these figures. The €537 600 would be better deployed on the motivators — progression, job design, supervision — or simply on absorbing the recruitment cost of the expansion.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
Halden Bikes sells only in its home market. The board must decide whether to move assembly to Country M, and the tariff is outside its control.

(a)

Calculate the total landed cost per unit of the Country M option, and compare it with the current unit cost of €42.

[5]

(b)

Calculate the annual saving at the current volume of 200 000 units, and express it as a percentage of the current total annual production cost.

[3]

(c)

Recalculate the landed cost per unit and the annual saving if the tariff rises to 25%, and comment on the significance of the change.

[3]

(d)

Recommend whether Halden Bikes should proceed, justifying your answer with reference to your calculations and to one non-financial factor.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Build the landed cost per unit from the components:

  • ex-works production: €28.00
  • import tariff at 18% of €28: €5.04
  • freight, insurance and handling: €3.50
  • expected rework cost: $0.04\times 6=€0.24$
  • set-up cost written off: $\dfrac{2\,400\,000}{5\times 200\,000}=€2.40$ (M1)(M1)(M1)

Total landed cost $=28.00+5.04+3.50+0.24+2.40=€39.18$ per unit. (M1)(A1)

This is €2.82 per unit below the current cost of €42.00. The €39.18 is also a best case: it excludes the cost of managing an overseas supplier — incoming quality inspection, extra safety stock for longer lead times, and currency exposure — none of which appears in the current €42.00.

(b) Annual saving $=2.82\times 200\,000=€564\,000$. (M1)(A1)

Current total annual production cost $=42\times 200\,000=€8\,400\,000$, so the saving is $\dfrac{564\,000}{8\,400\,000}\times 100=6.7\%$. (A1) The 6.7% is a saving on operating cost only; it takes no account of the one-off cost of closing the home line, such as redundancy payments and the write-down of plant, which would have to be recovered before the move pays back.

(c) With a 25% tariff the tariff component becomes $0.25\times 28=€7.00$, so the landed cost is $28.00+7.00+3.50+0.24+2.40=€41.14$ per unit. (M1)(A1)

The saving falls to €0.86 per unit, or $0.86\times 200\,000=€172\,000$ per year, which is 2.0% of current costs. (A1)

The headline saving of €14 per unit has been reduced to €2.82, and a plausible tariff change reduces it to €0.86. The decision therefore rests on a margin of less than €1 per unit on a product whose cost is €42, and the company would be committing to closing its home line, losing the skills and the flexibility that come with it, in exchange for a saving smaller than the annual variation in most input costs.

(d) Recommendation: do not proceed. (A1)

At the current tariff the saving is 6.7% of production cost, which is real but modest for a decision that is hard to reverse, and it exists only because the set-up cost is being spread over five years at the full current volume. If volumes fall, the per-unit write-off rises and the saving shrinks further; if the tariff rises to 25% as analysts expect, the saving falls to 2.0% and the case for moving effectively disappears. (A1)

The non-financial factor that matters most is reputational and political. Halden would be moving production out of its home country while continuing to sell only into that market, which exposes it to criticism from customers and employees and makes it a visible target when the tariff is next reviewed. A company that has moved its production abroad and is then faced with a further tariff increase cannot easily reverse the decision. The Country M option does offer lower costs and access to a larger labour supply, so a board that is confident of a large volume increase might reasonably revisit it, but on the figures available the saving is too small and too fragile to justify the commitment. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question is built on the gap between the headline number and the landed cost. The ex-works figure of €28 against a domestic cost of €42 suggests a saving of a third, which is large enough that many boards would stop analysing at that point. Building the landed cost removes most of it: the tariff applies to the ex-works value, freight and handling are unavoidable on every unit, a small failure rate carries a real expected cost, and the set-up cost has to be recovered over the volume actually produced. The saving collapses from €14 to €2.82 per unit, and that is before any consideration of what happens when the tariff changes.

The sensitivity part is the substance of the question. The single largest component after the ex-works cost is the tariff, and it is outside the company's control. A rise from 18% to 25% is well within the range that governments make for reasons that have nothing to do with this company, and it reduces the saving to €0.86 per unit. A business that has closed its home line cannot respond to that by moving production back: the decision is effectively irreversible, while the cost that most threatens it can change at a year's notice. That asymmetry between a reversible threat and an irreversible response is the argument against proceeding, and it is a general principle rather than a number.

It is worth noticing that the analysis is not an argument against locating production abroad in principle. Country M does have substantially lower labour costs, and if volumes grew sharply the per-unit set-up write-off would fall and the case would improve. What the figures show is that at the current volume and with the current tariff, the margin is too thin to carry the risk being taken, and that the decision should be revisited if either the volume or the tariff environment changes in the company's favour.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
Priya and Tom must decide whether Nettle & Vine should accept the supermarket's exclusive own-label contract.

(a)

Explain two business functions at Nettle & Vine and how each function contributes to the value the business adds.

[4]

(b)

Using the customer table, calculate the mean and the median annual spend per account. Then calculate value added, value added per litre and value added per employee for Option A and for the supermarket contract.

[5]

(c)

Using SWOT analysis, evaluate whether Nettle & Vine should accept the supermarket contract. Refer to your calculations and to the objectives of the two founders.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Award up to four marks for two business functions, each explained in the context of Nettle & Vine.

Operations (production). The operations function is the transformation process: it converts bought-in inputs that cost EUR 1.20 a litre into bottled cordial that sells for EUR 4.00 a litre. Almost all of the value the business adds is created here, because the recipe, the brewing and the bottling turn cheap ingredients into a product a customer will pay a premium for. (A1)(A1)

Marketing. The marketing function is what allows the business to charge EUR 4.00 rather than a commodity price. The Nettle & Vine name, the founders' signatures, the story of the recipe and the refusal to use imported fruit are all marketing decisions, and they are the reason 40 independent retailers buy the cordial instead of a cheaper own-label alternative. Marketing therefore captures the value that operations creates. (A1)(A1)

Also creditable: finance (arranging and servicing the EUR 200 000 loan and costing the supermarket contract), human resources (recruiting and training the eight staff the contract would need), and product development (Priya's recipes and the product range).

(b) Customer data. Total annual spend of the 40 accounts is EUR 240 000, so the mean is $EUR 240 000 / 40 = EUR 6 000$. The median is EUR 2 400, because 25 of the 40 accounts spend only EUR 2 400 and the five largest spend EUR 20 000 each. (M1)(A1)

The mean is 2.5 times the median, so the 'average customer' is not a typical customer. The five largest accounts alone provide EUR 100 000, or 41.7% of trade revenue. The business is already more concentrated than the mean figure suggests. (A1)

Value added = revenue minus bought-in materials and services.

Option A: revenue $= 60 000 \times EUR 4.00 = EUR 240 000$; bought-in $= 60 000 \times EUR 1.20 = EUR 72 000$; value added $= EUR 168 000$. Value added per litre $= EUR 168 000 / 60 000 = EUR 2.80$. Value added per employee $= EUR 168 000 / 6 = EUR 28 000$. (M1)(A1)

Supermarket contract: revenue $= 180 000 \times EUR 1.55 = EUR 279 000$; bought-in $= 180 000 \times EUR 0.40 = EUR 72 000$; value added $= EUR 207 000$. Value added per litre $= EUR 207 000 / 180 000 = EUR 1.15$. Value added per employee $= EUR 207 000 / 8 = EUR 25 875$. (M1)(A1)

The two measures disagree. The contract adds more value in total (EUR 207 000 against EUR 168 000) and produces three times the volume, but it adds only EUR 1.15 a litre against EUR 2.80, a fall of 59%, and less value per employee. The contract buys volume with a much thinner margin.

(c) Indicative evaluation. A SWOT built from the case:

Strengths: a distinctive own brand; Priya's recipe; 40 loyal trade accounts; a premium price of EUR 4.00 a litre; a site that is full and profitable.
Weaknesses: no space to grow; no financial analysis; 42% of trade revenue from five accounts; only six staff; the founders' pay is low.
Opportunities: the supermarket contract would give three years of guaranteed volume; the craft drinks market is growing; a rival's takeover shows that small producers are attractive to larger buyers.
Threats: the contract is exclusive and would end the trade business; the brand would disappear from the bottles; the supermarket sets and reviews the price annually; a rival has cut its trade prices.

The quantitative case is closer than it first appears. The contract adds EUR 39 000 more value in total, but the EUR 200 000 loan costs EUR 16 000 a year in interest, so the gain falls to EUR 23 000, about 14% of Option A's value added. The supermarket may review the price after one year, and a cut of even 10% (to EUR 1.40) would reduce the contract's value added by EUR 18 000 and leave the business barely ahead of doing nothing while having given up its brand, its recipe and its independence. The loan also requires personal guarantees from both founders.

The SWOT shows that the contract removes the business's main weakness (no capacity to grow) by destroying its main strength (the brand). The descriptive statistics make the same point from the other direction: the business already depends on five large accounts, and the contract would replace that with dependence on a single customer that sets the price. Priya's objective is to protect the recipe and the identity of the business; Tom's is security and a proper income. The contract delivers Tom's objective only while the supermarket chooses to keep the price.

A supported conclusion is required. Rejecting the contract, or negotiating a non-exclusive, shorter or higher-priced deal, is creditworthy if the reasoning is consistent with the candidate's own figures. A conclusion that rests only on 'growth is good', or only on 'the brand matters', is not.
questions.explanation:
The case is built so that the obvious answer - grow - is supported by the headline figures and contradicted by the analysis. The contract triples the volume, raises revenue from EUR 240 000 to EUR 279 000, and adds more value in total than Option A. Tom's case is not stupid, and the item is designed so that a candidate who simply says 'the supermarket is exploiting them' has not done the work.

The lever is that adding value can be measured in two defensible ways, and they point in opposite directions. Per litre, Option A adds EUR 2.80 and the contract adds EUR 1.15, a collapse of 59%: the contract converts a premium brand into a low-margin contract manufacturer. In total, the contract adds more (EUR 207 000 against EUR 168 000), because three times the volume of a thinner margin can still be more value. Neither measure is wrong, and the decision cannot be made without deciding which one the founders are trying to maximise - which is a question about the purpose of the business, not about the arithmetic.

The second layer is financing. The EUR 200 000 loan costs EUR 16 000 a year, which cuts the gain from EUR 39 000 to EUR 23 000. Because the supermarket may review the price after a year, a modest cut wipes that out. The commitment - personal guarantees, a three-year exclusive contract, the loss of the brand - is irreversible in a way the benefit is not.

The descriptive statistics are not decoration. The mean customer spend of EUR 6 000 is two and a half times the median of EUR 2 400, because five accounts dominate. That tells the student the business is already concentrated, so replacing 40 accounts with one is not a reduction in risk but an increase in it.

Classic wrong turns: comparing revenue rather than value added; treating the loan interest as a bought-in cost inside the value added calculation; praising the contract for creating two jobs without noticing that value added per employee falls; and answering (c) with a general discussion of supermarkets that never uses the figures.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
Nia and Rob must decide whether the funding plan in their business plan is realistic enough to open Wagtail & Co.

(a)

Distinguish between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure, using examples from the case, and explain why the distinction matters when a start-up is deciding how much finance it needs.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the total finance required at start-up, showing the capital expenditure, the working capital requirement and the contingency separately.

[5]

(c)

Using the financial section of the business plan, evaluate whether the funding plan is realistic, referring to the bank's lending limit, the grant, the lease offer and Rob's aunt's proposal.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets that will be used in the business for more than a year - it buys something the business keeps. Revenue expenditure is spending on the day-to-day running of the business, which is consumed within the year. (A1)(A1)

In this case the five items in the table are all capital expenditure: the conversion of the unit, the grooming equipment, the van, the software and the signage are assets the business will use for several years. The rent, wages, utilities, insurance, dog food and marketing are revenue expenditure, because they are incurred month by month and create no lasting asset. (A1)

The distinction matters because the two types of spending have to be financed differently. Capital expenditure is a large, one-off sum that a bank will often lend against, because the asset can be secured. Revenue expenditure recurs every month, is not secured by an asset, and must be financed from cash or from working capital - so it is easy to underestimate and hard to borrow against. (A1)

(b) Capital expenditure $= EUR 52 000 + EUR 16 000 + EUR 28 000 + EUR 6 000 + EUR 8 000 = EUR 110 000$. (M1)(A1)

Monthly running costs $= EUR 3 000 + EUR 7 800 + EUR 1 200 + EUR 400 + EUR 4 600 + EUR 500 = EUR 17 500$. Three months of running costs must be financed before the business earns anything, so working capital $= 3 \times EUR 17 500 = EUR 52 500$. (M1)(A1)

Contingency $= 10\% \times (EUR 110 000 + EUR 52 500) = 10\% \times EUR 162 500 = EUR 16 250$. Total finance required $= EUR 110 000 + EUR 52 500 + EUR 16 250 = EUR 178 750$. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation, using the financial section of the business plan.

The plan looks balanced on its own assumptions: it claims EUR 180 000 of funding against a requirement of EUR 178 750, a margin of EUR 1 250. But two of the three funding assumptions are wrong.

The bank will lend at most 60% of the value of the capital items, which is $60\% \times EUR 110 000 = EUR 66 000$, not the EUR 115 000 requested. The grant is capped at EUR 12 000, not EUR 20 000. The realistic funding is therefore $EUR 45 000 + EUR 66 000 + EUR 12 000 = EUR 123 000$, against a requirement of EUR 178 750. The shortfall is EUR 55 750, and the plan's apparent EUR 1 250 surplus becomes a EUR 55 750 hole. (M1)(A1)

The shortfall is almost entirely a working-capital problem. The business needs EUR 52 500 of cash to survive three months with no income, and the bank will not lend against it. The founders have focused on the visible assets and underestimated the cost of simply keeping the doors open.

The lease offer helps the capital side but not enough. Leasing the grooming equipment and the van (EUR 44 000) would cut capital expenditure to EUR 66 000, but it adds EUR 980 a month to running costs, raising monthly costs to EUR 18 480 and working capital to EUR 55 440. With a 10% contingency on EUR 121 440, the total requirement becomes EUR 133 584. The bank's limit then falls to EUR 39 600, so available funding is EUR 96 600 and the shortfall is EUR 36 984. Leasing reduces the gap by about EUR 19 000 but increases the monthly cost permanently.

Rob's aunt's EUR 56 000 would close the gap, but it costs 25% of the business, which both founders have said they do not want to give up. It also transfers a quarter of any future growth to someone who is contributing money rather than work.

A supported conclusion is required. A candidate who recommends delaying the opening, phasing the spend, reducing the contingency, or accepting the aunt's money, and who justifies it with the figures, should be credited. The key judgement is that the plan is not realistic as written: it understates the finance needed by about EUR 55 750 and misunderstands how a bank lends to a start-up.
questions.explanation:
The question is designed so that the plan appears to work. EUR 180 000 of funding against a requirement of EUR 178 750 is a surplus of EUR 1 250, and a candidate who checks only the addition will conclude that the plan is sound. The trap is that the funding side contains assumptions the case has already contradicted: the bank's lending rule and the grant cap are stated plainly, and both reduce the money actually available.

The deeper point, and the reason the item sits in Unit 3.1 rather than in sources of finance, is the difference between capital and revenue expenditure and what it means for how much finance a start-up actually needs. The visible, exciting items - the conversion, the van, the equipment - are the ones founders plan for. The invisible item is working capital: EUR 52 500 of rent, wages, insurance and consumables that must be paid for three months before the business earns a penny. Banks will lend against a van; they will not lend against next quarter's wages. So the shortfall is concentrated precisely where borrowing is hardest.

The lease option is a genuine second lever. Converting EUR 44 000 of capital expenditure into a monthly payment reduces the upfront requirement from EUR 178 750 to EUR 133 584 and cuts the shortfall from EUR 55 750 to EUR 36 984 - but it raises the monthly running cost and therefore the working capital requirement too. Students who treat leasing as a pure saving have missed the interaction between the two.

Classic wrong turns: adding only the capital items and reporting EUR 110 000 as the finance required; accepting the EUR 115 000 loan; forgetting the contingency; and concluding that the aunt's offer solves everything without noticing that it costs a quarter of the business, which the founders have said they will not give up.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.question:
The board of Pennine Workwear must decide whether to keep the new production process.

(a)

Explain, with reference to the transformation process, how the operations function at Pennine Workwear adds value to the business.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the labour productivity and the value added per garment in a typical month before the change and in a typical month since the change. Comment on what your figures show.

[5]

(c)

Using descriptive statistics on the defect-rate data, evaluate whether Pennine Workwear should keep the new production process.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Pennine Workwear operates a transformation process. The inputs are bought-in fabric, thread and components costing EUR 7 a garment, together with 2 400 hours of direct labour a month and the use of the factory and machinery. The process is cutting, sewing, finishing, inspecting and packing. The outputs are finished protective garments sold at EUR 18 each, which for many customers must also be safe, durable and compliant with industry standards.

The operations function adds value in two ways. First, it converts EUR 7 of materials into a garment that sells for EUR 18 - the transformation itself is where the added value is created. Second, it is responsible for the quality and reliability that make the garment worth buying: a protective jacket that fails in use is worthless, so the inspection and finishing stages protect the price the business can charge. Operations therefore supports the whole business strategy, not just the production line.

(b) Labour productivity = garments produced per direct labour hour.

Before the change: $12 000 / 2 400 = 5.0$ garments per labour hour. (M1)(A1)
Since the change: $15 000 / 2 500 = 6.0$ garments per labour hour. (A1)
That is a rise of $(6.0 - 5.0) / 5.0 = 20\%$, which is the figure the operations manager is reporting.

Value added = revenue minus bought-in materials minus rework cost.

Before the change: revenue $= 12 000 \times EUR 18 = EUR 216 000$; materials $= 12 000 \times EUR 7 = EUR 84 000$; defects $= 2\% \times 12 000 = 240$ garments, rework $= 240 \times EUR 4 = EUR 960$. Value added $= EUR 216 000 - EUR 84 000 - EUR 960 = EUR 131 040$, or $EUR 131 040 / 12 000 = EUR 10.92$ per garment. (M1)(A1)

Since the change: revenue $= 15 000 \times EUR 18 = EUR 270 000$, less 450 garments sold as seconds at EUR 9 instead of EUR 18, a loss of $450 \times EUR 9 = EUR 4 050$, so EUR 265 950; materials $= 15 000 \times EUR 7 = EUR 105 000$; defects $= 7\% \times 15 000 = 1 050$ garments, rework $= 1 050 \times EUR 4 = EUR 4 200$. Value added $= EUR 265 950 - EUR 105 000 - EUR 4 200 = EUR 156 750$, or $EUR 156 750 / 15 000 = EUR 10.45$ per garment. (M1)(A1)

The two measures disagree. Labour productivity is up 20%, but value added per garment has fallen from EUR 10.92 to EUR 10.45, a fall of about 4.3%. Total value added has risen, from EUR 131 040 to EUR 156 750, but only because 25% more garments are being made. Each garment now adds less value than before, because the cost of rework and of selling seconds has risen faster than the extra output is worth. Efficiency has improved; effectiveness has not.

(c) Indicative evaluation, using descriptive statistics on the twelve monthly defect rates.

The mean defect rate for the year is $(2.1 + 1.8 + 2.3 + 1.9 + 2.2 + 2.1 + 6.8 + 7.1 + 6.4 + 7.6 + 8.1 + 7.4) / 12 = 55.8 / 12 = 4.65\%$. Taken alone, that looks acceptable. The median is 4.35% and the range is $8.1 - 1.8 = 6.3$ percentage points. (M1)(A1)

The mean is misleading. Splitting the data at the change gives a mean of 2.07% for months 1 to 6 and 7.23% for months 7 to 12. The process did not drift; it stepped from about 2% to about 7% at the moment the change was introduced, and the annual mean of 4.65% describes no month that actually occurred. This is the classic trap of a summary statistic that conceals a structural break.

Two of the largest customers, together worth about 30% of sales, have complained, and one has asked for a meeting. Three experienced machinists have left in four months, which will put further pressure on quality. The operations manager's bonus depends on productivity, which explains why he is recommending a further increase in line speed, but his measure ignores the cost of defects and returns.

Conclusion: the change should not be kept in its present form. The productivity gain is real, but it has been bought by cutting the quality checks that protect the EUR 18 price. A supported conclusion is required; a candidate who recommends keeping the change but restoring the inspection stage, and justifies this from the figures, is equally creditworthy.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the difference between efficiency and effectiveness, which is the heart of Unit 5.1. Efficiency asks whether the business is doing things right - more output per hour, lower unit cost. Effectiveness asks whether it is doing the right things - making something the customer will pay for and keep buying. The operations manager has improved the first and damaged the second, and his bonus is tied to the measure that improved.

The arithmetic is deliberately arranged so that the trap is visible but easy to miss. Labour productivity rises by exactly 20%, which is the figure the case quotes, and total value added also rises, from EUR 131 040 to EUR 156 750. A student who checks only these two numbers concludes that the change is a success. The figure that contradicts them is value added per garment, which falls from EUR 10.92 to EUR 10.45 because the cost of rework and of selling seconds rises faster than the extra output is worth. Twenty-five per cent more garments are being made, and each one is worth slightly less.

The descriptive statistics add a second, sharper point. The annual mean defect rate of 4.65% looks unremarkable, but no month had a defect rate near it: the process ran at about 2% and then stepped to about 7%. A summary statistic that averages across a structural break describes nothing real. This is why the question supplies twelve monthly figures rather than two averages, and it is what separates a candidate who can calculate a mean from one who can interpret it.

The qualitative evidence - two large customers complaining, three machinists leaving, a bonus tied to the wrong measure - is there to support the evaluation rather than to replace it. The strongest answers notice that the operations manager's incentive and the company's interest have diverged, which is why the recommendation is not simply 'work harder on quality' but 'restore the check that the change removed'.

Classic wrong turns: treating a 20% productivity gain as automatically good; using total value added instead of value added per unit; and reporting the annual mean defect rate without splitting it at the change.
